questions.title: Spring Boot Auto-Configuration
questions.question: What is Spring Boot auto-configuration and how does it work?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Classpath scanning:** auto-config reads what's on the classpath to decide what to configure
- **Conditional annotations:** `@ConditionalOnClass`, `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` are the core mechanism
- **AutoConfiguration.imports / spring.factories:** know where auto-configs are registered
- **Override-ability:** user-defined beans take priority — auto-config backs off
- **Depth signal:** mention that debug=true shows the conditions report
- **Red flag:** saying "Spring Boot just magically configures things" without knowing the mechanism

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Spring Boot auto-configuration automatically configures your application based on the jars on the classpath. When you add spring-boot-starter-web, Spring Boot detects Spring MVC and Tomcat are present and configures a DispatcherServlet, an embedded Tomcat server, and Jackson — all without you writing a single line of config.

The mechanism works through `@EnableAutoConfiguration`, which is included in `@SpringBootApplication`. It loads a list of configuration classes from `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` in Spring Boot 3, or `spring.factories` in Boot 2. Each of those classes uses conditional annotations — mainly `@ConditionalOnClass` to check if a library is present, and `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` to back off if you've already defined your own bean.

The key design principle is: sensible defaults you can always override. If you define your own `DataSource` bean, Spring Boot detects it and skips creating one. Run your app with `debug=true` to see the full conditions report — it shows exactly what was configured and what was skipped and why.

speakable_v2.hook: Spring Boot auto-configuration automatically configures your application based on the jars on the classpath.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Run your app with debug=true to see the full conditions report — it shows exactly what was configured and what was skipped and why.

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Trigger for auto-config:** it's the annotation that activates the whole mechanism
- **`AutoConfigurationImportSelector`:** knows this class is what does the actual work
- **Part of `@SpringBootApplication`:** you rarely use it standalone
- **`exclude` attribute:** can disable specific auto-configurations
- **Red flag:** confusing it with `@ComponentScan` — they are different concerns

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`@EnableAutoConfiguration` is the annotation that triggers Spring Boot's auto-configuration mechanism. You normally never write it directly — it's one of the three annotations composed inside `@SpringBootApplication`.

Internally, it imports `AutoConfigurationImportSelector`, which reads the list of all available auto-configuration classes and evaluates their conditions against your application's classpath and context. Classes that pass their conditions are loaded as regular `@Configuration` classes.

You can use its `exclude` attribute to turn off specific auto-configurations — for example, `@EnableAutoConfiguration(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)` if you're building an app with no database. This is cleaner than completely disabling all auto-configuration.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: @EnableAutoConfiguration is the annotation that triggers Spring Boot's auto-configuration mechanism.
speakable_v2.cap: This is cleaner than completely disabling all auto-configuration.

questions.title: @SpringBootApplication Annotation
questions.question: What is @SpringBootApplication and what annotations does it combine?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Three composed annotations:** `@SpringBootConfiguration`, `@EnableAutoConfiguration`, `@ComponentScan`
- **Placement matters:** must be at the root package so `@ComponentScan` picks up all sub-packages
- **Customisation:** `exclude`, `scanBasePackages` attributes
- **Depth signal:** `@SpringBootConfiguration` is just `@Configuration` with a different name
- **Red flag:** not knowing which three annotations it combines

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`@SpringBootApplication` is a convenience meta-annotation that combines three annotations into one. First, `@SpringBootConfiguration`, which marks the class as a configuration source — it's essentially `@Configuration`. Second, `@EnableAutoConfiguration`, which activates Spring Boot's auto-configuration mechanism. Third, `@ComponentScan`, which tells Spring to scan the current package and all sub-packages for components like `@Service`, `@Controller`, and `@Repository`.

You place it on your main application class, and the placement determines the base package for component scanning — which is why the main class is usually at the root of your package hierarchy. You can customise it: use `exclude` to disable specific auto-configurations, or `scanBasePackages` if your components live outside the main class's package.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: @SpringBootApplication is a convenience meta-annotation that combines three annotations into one.
speakable_v2.cap: You can customise it: use exclude to disable specific auto-configurations, or scanBasePackages if your components live outside the main class's package.

questions.title: spring.factories Mechanism
questions.question: What is META-INF/spring.factories and how does Spring Boot use it?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **SPI mechanism:** it's Spring Boot's service-provider interface for extensibility
- **Key-value format:** fully-qualified interface name maps to comma-separated implementation class names
- **Boot 2 vs Boot 3:** Boot 3 replaced it with `AutoConfiguration.imports` for auto-configs
- **Still used in Boot 3:** for other extension points like `ApplicationListener`, `FailureAnalyzer`
- **Red flag:** thinking it's been completely removed — it still exists, just auto-config no longer uses it

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`META-INF/spring.factories` is a properties file that Spring Boot uses as a service-provider registry. Libraries declare their extension implementations here, and Spring Boot discovers them at startup without the application needing to explicitly import them.

The format is simple: a fully-qualified interface or annotation name as the key, mapped to one or more implementation class names as values. For example, `EnableAutoConfiguration` maps to all auto-configuration classes that Spring Boot ships with.

In Spring Boot 3, auto-configuration class registration was moved to a dedicated file — `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` — which is faster and simpler. But `spring.factories` is still used for other extension points like `ApplicationListener`, `EnvironmentPostProcessor`, and `FailureAnalyzer`. If you're building a custom Spring Boot starter, you'll still interact with these files.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## File Format

```properties
# META-INF/spring.factories
org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.EnableAutoConfiguration=\
  org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration,\
  org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.web.servlet.WebMvcAutoConfiguration

org.springframework.context.ApplicationListener=\
  org.springframework.boot.builder.ParentContextCloserApplicationListener
```

## Boot 2 vs Boot 3

In Boot 3, auto-configuration entries moved out of `spring.factories` into:
```
META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports
```

This file is a plain list — one class per line:
```
org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration
org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.web.servlet.WebMvcAutoConfiguration
```

Advantages: faster parsing, no string escaping, cleaner diffs.

## What Still Uses spring.factories in Boot 3

- `ApplicationListener`
- `ApplicationContextInitializer`
- `EnvironmentPostProcessor`
- `FailureAnalyzer`
- `SpringApplicationRunListener`

## Production Reality

When building a custom starter library, you declare your auto-configuration in `AutoConfiguration.imports` (Boot 3) or `spring.factories` (Boot 2) — not in `@Import` statements. This keeps the library's internals decoupled from the consuming application.

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Replacement for spring.factories for auto-configs in Boot 3:** know the migration direction
- **One class per line:** simpler format, no escaping
- **Processed by `ImportCandidates`:** the internal loader class changed
- **Backwards compatible:** Boot 3 still reads `spring.factories` for non-auto-config extensions
- **Depth signal:** mention this matters when migrating Boot 2 starters to Boot 3

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
In Spring Boot 3, auto-configuration class registration was moved from `spring.factories` to a dedicated file: `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`. The format is simpler — just one fully-qualified class name per line, no key-value syntax, no backslash continuation.

The motivation was performance and clarity. Parsing a plain list is faster than parsing a properties file with escaped multi-line values, and the diffs in version control are cleaner. When Boot 3 loads auto-configurations, it reads this file instead of scanning `spring.factories` for the `EnableAutoConfiguration` key.

This matters in practice when you're migrating a custom Spring Boot 2 starter to Boot 3 — you need to create this new file and move your auto-configuration class entries there. The rest of the extension points like `ApplicationListener` still use `spring.factories`.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## File Location and Format

```
src/main/resources/META-INF/spring/
  org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports
```

Content (one class per line):
```
com.example.starter.FooAutoConfiguration
com.example.starter.BarAutoConfiguration
```

Compare with the Boot 2 equivalent in `spring.factories`:
```properties
org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.EnableAutoConfiguration=\
  com.example.starter.FooAutoConfiguration,\
  com.example.starter.BarAutoConfiguration
```

## Who Reads It

`ImportCandidates` (replacing `SpringFactoriesLoader` for this purpose) loads the file. It aggregates entries from all jars on the classpath, so multiple starters can each contribute their own classes.

## Migrating a Boot 2 Starter to Boot 3

1. Create `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`
2. Move auto-config class names into it, one per line
3. Annotate your auto-config class with `@AutoConfiguration` instead of `@Configuration`
4. Keep `spring.factories` for non-auto-config entries (listeners, etc.)

## Production Reality

If you ship an internal library used across multiple Spring Boot services, migrating to the new format is a hard requirement for Boot 3 compatibility. The old `spring.factories` auto-config entries are silently ignored in Boot 3.

speakable_v2.cap: The rest of the extension points like ApplicationListener still use spring.factories.

questions.title: @ConditionalOnClass
questions.question: What is @ConditionalOnClass annotation and when is it used?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Classpath condition:** activates configuration only when a class is present on the classpath
- **Starter dependency pattern:** adding a starter brings in the class, which triggers the auto-config
- **`value` vs `name`:** `value` requires the class to be resolvable at compile time; `name` (string) avoids that
- **Paired with `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`:** typically used together
- **Red flag:** thinking it checks at runtime whether an object exists — it's a classpath check at startup

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`@ConditionalOnClass` registers a bean or configuration class only if a specific class is present on the classpath. It's the foundational condition that makes the starter pattern work: you add a starter dependency, which brings a library's classes onto the classpath, which triggers `@ConditionalOnClass` to activate the corresponding auto-configuration.

For example, `DataSourceAutoConfiguration` is annotated with `@ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class)`. The moment you add a JDBC driver or spring-boot-starter-data-jpa to your project, `DataSource.class` appears on the classpath and the auto-configuration activates.

When the class you're checking for isn't guaranteed to be on your compile classpath — for instance, you're writing a library — use the `name` attribute with a string class name instead of `value` with a class literal, to avoid compile-time failures.

speakable_v2.hook: @ConditionalOnClass registers a bean or configuration class only if a specific class is present on the classpath.

questions.title: @ConditionalOnBean
questions.question: What is @ConditionalOnBean and how does it work?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Application context condition:** checks if a bean of a given type already exists in the context
- **Opposite of `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`:** creates bean only when the dependency IS present
- **Order sensitivity:** beans checked must be registered before this condition is evaluated
- **Common use:** wiring optional features — "add rate limiter only if a CacheManager bean exists"
- **Red flag:** assuming it can check for beans defined later in the context — ordering matters

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`@ConditionalOnBean` creates a bean only if another bean of a specified type is already present in the Spring application context. It's the complement of `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` — rather than backing off when a bean exists, it activates only when a dependency is present.

A common use case is optional integrations: imagine you have a metrics publisher that only makes sense if a `MeterRegistry` bean is registered. You annotate the publisher's `@Bean` method with `@ConditionalOnBean(MeterRegistry.class)`, and it auto-wires itself only when Micrometer is on the classpath and configured.

The critical gotcha is ordering. The bean you're checking for must be registered before Spring evaluates this condition. If you're using it in a user-defined `@Configuration` class rather than an auto-configuration, the order is less predictable. It works most reliably in auto-configuration classes, which have explicit ordering via `@AutoConfigureAfter`.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: @ConditionalOnBean creates a bean only if another bean of a specified type is already present in the Spring application context.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: It works most reliably in auto-configuration classes, which have explicit ordering via @AutoConfigureAfter.

questions.title: @ConditionalOnMissingBean
questions.question: What is @ConditionalOnMissingBean and why is it important for auto-configuration?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Override mechanism:** the reason you can customise any auto-configured bean without disabling auto-config
- **Convention over configuration:** Boot provides defaults; you override by simply defining your own bean
- **Applied to auto-config beans:** almost every auto-configured `@Bean` method has this
- **Gotcha:** doesn't work between `@Bean` methods in the same `@Configuration` class
- **Red flag:** thinking you need to exclude auto-config to customise — just define your own bean

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`@ConditionalOnMissingBean` creates a bean only if no bean of that type already exists in the Spring application context. It's the annotation that makes Spring Boot's entire auto-configuration system customisable without being forced to disable it.

Every auto-configured bean uses this annotation. When Spring Boot's `DataSourceAutoConfiguration` creates a `DataSource` bean, it checks first with `@ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class)`. If you've defined your own `DataSource` — perhaps with a custom connection pool size — Spring Boot detects it and skips its default. No exclusions needed, no XML overrides, just define your bean.

The one gotcha to know: it doesn't work between `@Bean` methods in the same `@Configuration` class. If you define a custom bean and the auto-configured fallback in the same class, the condition evaluates before either bean in the class is registered. The solution is to keep them in separate configuration classes.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: @ConditionalOnMissingBean creates a bean only if no bean of that type already exists in the Spring application context.
speakable_v2.cap: The solution is to keep them in separate configuration classes.

questions.title: @ConditionalOnProperty
questions.question: How does @ConditionalOnProperty enable property-based conditional configuration?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Feature flags via properties:** activate/deactivate beans from application.properties
- **`havingValue` attribute:** condition passes only when property equals this value
- **`matchIfMissing`:** what happens when the property isn't set at all
- **Common pattern:** `feature.x.enabled=true` toggles a whole feature's beans
- **Red flag:** not knowing about `matchIfMissing` — matters for safe defaults

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`@ConditionalOnProperty` registers a bean only when a specific property in your configuration has a particular value. It's the standard way to implement feature flags in Spring Boot — you expose a property like `app.cache.enabled=true`, and the caching beans activate only when it's set to true.

The annotation has two key attributes beyond the property name. `havingValue` specifies what value the property must equal for the condition to pass. `matchIfMissing` controls what happens if the property isn't set at all — if `matchIfMissing = true`, the condition passes even when the property is absent, making the feature on-by-default.

This is cleaner than using profiles for feature toggling because profiles are environment-scoped, while properties can be changed per-deployment without rebuilding the app.

speakable_v2.hook: @ConditionalOnProperty registers a bean only when a specific property in your configuration has a particular value.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: This is cleaner than using profiles for feature toggling because profiles are environment-scoped, while properties can be changed per-deployment without rebuilding the app.

questions.title: Excluding Auto-Configuration
questions.question: How do you exclude specific auto-configurations?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Three ways:** annotation `exclude`, annotation `excludeName`, properties
- **When to use:** class not wanted on classpath but pulled in transitively by another starter
- **Better alternative first:** consider overriding with your own bean before excluding
- **`excludeName` for optional deps:** when the class may not be on your compile classpath
- **Red flag:** using exclusion as the first resort instead of bean override

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
You can exclude auto-configurations in three ways. The most common is via the `exclude` attribute on `@SpringBootApplication`, passing the auto-configuration class directly. The second is `excludeName`, which takes a string class name — useful when the class isn't guaranteed to be on your compile classpath, such as when a library is an optional transitive dependency.

The third way is via `application.properties` using `spring.autoconfigure.exclude`, which is useful when you need to disable something without changing your main class — for example, in a test configuration.

Before reaching for exclusion, consider whether overriding is better. If the issue is that Spring Boot creates a bean with wrong defaults, just define your own bean — `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` will cause auto-config to back off. Exclusion is most appropriate when you want to prevent a whole auto-configuration from running at all, not just customise its output.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Method 1: Annotation exclude (preferred)

```java
@SpringBootApplication(exclude = {
    DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class,
    HibernateJpaAutoConfiguration.class
})
public class Application { ... }
```

Requires the class to be on your classpath (compile-time reference).

## Method 2: Annotation excludeName

```java
@SpringBootApplication(excludeName = {
    "org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration"
})
public class Application { ... }
```

Use when the class may not be on your compile classpath.

## Method 3: Properties (flexible for environments)

```properties
# application.properties
spring.autoconfigure.exclude=\
  org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration,\
  org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.security.servlet.SecurityAutoConfiguration
```

This is useful in test configurations or environment-specific property files.

## Common Exclusion Scenarios

| Situation | What to exclude |
|---|---|
| No database in app | `DataSourceAutoConfiguration` |
| Custom security config | `SecurityAutoConfiguration` |
| Non-web batch app | `WebMvcAutoConfiguration` |
| Custom data source | Don't exclude — override with your bean |

## Production Reality

A common trap: excluding `DataSourceAutoConfiguration` but forgetting to also exclude `HibernateJpaAutoConfiguration` and `DataSourceTransactionManagerAutoConfiguration`. They depend on `DataSource` and fail with confusing errors if left enabled without it.

speakable_v2.cap: Exclusion is most appropriate when you want to prevent a whole auto-configuration from running at all, not just customise its output.
